messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Stress: Stress, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert, a 62-year-old European American bank teller, came to treatment after months of feeling unable to settle back into ordinary life since the day he accidentally caused a serious injury to another man. He still described that afternoon in the bank lobby with painful clarity: he had been reaching to help an older customer who had stumbled near the counter, lost his balance in the rush of trying to steady him, and in the confusion the man fell hard and was badly hurt. Robert had never imagined that a brief moment of misplaced contact could end with another person lying on the floor in pain, and ever since, that scene had sat at the center of his mind. What stayed with him was not only the image of the fall but the instant terror he felt when he realized he had been the one who set it in motion. Even now, remembering it brought back the same dread in his chest, along with sudden fragments of the memory that would flash up without warning and vanish before he could push them away.

In the weeks that followed, Robert began to judge himself harshly. He had come to believe that he was inadequate, that his reactions showed he was a lousy coper, and that something in him had permanently changed for the worse. He found himself replaying the incident in the middle of otherwise ordinary moments, and each time the guilt felt fresh and crushing, as if the event were still unfolding and he were still failing to prevent it. Those appraisals did not stay abstract: they shaped how he moved through the day. At work, in his narrow space behind the teller window, he became wary of customers he knew from the neighborhood and especially of longtime account holders who reminded him of the injured man. A familiar face at the counter could suddenly make him feel as though he had been exposed as careless and untrustworthy, and that sense of being fundamentally flawed made him pull back even more. He avoided lingering conversations and became guarded around people who knew him well, because their recognition seemed to press on the same shame.

The more Robert saw himself as damaged and inept, the more often the memory intruded. A customer’s brief remark, the sight of an older man shifting awkwardly in line, or an unexpected brush of someone’s hand against his arm could bring the event back with startling force. The fragments arrived as if from nowhere, and once they did, the terror and guilt flooded in together. When that happened, Robert’s body reacted as though danger were present again. He became superalert and watchful, scanning the lobby, the doorway, and the movements of people around him. He could not relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, and by evening he was still keyed up, unable to let his guard down. At night he had difficulty falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert, as if sleep itself would leave him unprepared for the next mistake or the next sudden reminder.

That state of constant vigilance began to shape what he noticed in the world. Because he was always on guard, he was especially sensitive to stress, to any moment when the branch got busy or tensions rose at the counter, and those situations made him even more likely to feel that he was on the verge of another failure. In turn, his alertness made him track the people and sensations around him more closely, which meant that small things could become potent triggers. A coworker touching his shoulder from behind without warning in the break room, or a hand resting unexpectedly on his arm while he stood beside the copier, could jolt him back into the same surge of alarm he had felt at the time of the accident. After each such moment, he became more convinced that he could not trust himself to stay composed, and that renewed shame sent him back into the memory again, where the guilt and terror were waiting in full force. The cycle had narrowed his life: he avoided being touched unprepared, kept his distance from familiar people when he could, and carried the strain home with him. His marriage had become quieter and more strained because even in his own kitchen he seemed braced for something to go wrong.

By the time he sought help, Robert was exhausted by the effort of staying composed. He wanted relief from the replaying scenes, from the way his mind kept throwing him back into that one disastrous moment, and from the fear that his watchfulness was becoming the only way he knew how to keep himself and others safe. What brought him in was not a single crisis but the realization that he was living as if he were still in the lobby, still waiting for something terrible to happen. He was most afraid that if he let his guard down, he would fail again and hurt someone else; he was most hoping to learn how to sleep, relax, and face his days without the constant sense that he was permanently broken.
